Around 1:00 I bumped into four other birders in the parking lot of the school adjacent to the park. Together we had a pair of apparent Cassin’s Finches in a tree at (37.2834434, -121.9985356). While walking along the bike path we noticed a small, buffy sparrow with big head and a short tail scurry behind a bush near (37.4355120, -122.0923952). It was secretive in behavior…it would scurry or take low long hops between bushes then stand perfectly still. Crouched stance most of the time and very quiet. Large head and large bill, with a gently slope that made a smooth ongoing line (seemingly no angle between bill and forehead). Fairly plain face with thin brown streak behind the eye, dark brown crown with pale center stripe, and pale complete eye ring. Intricate pattern on back/wings with reddish spots in center of each feather, edged with black. Seemed like it had a short yellow eyebrow/streak above the front of the eye. Pale-orange/buffy face and belly. No streaking on belly/chest, but some faint buffy streaks near armpit and lower back flank. By the time we tried to get pictures through our binoculars it was on the move, heading under another bush and then flew low across the pave path to the steep hillside next to the salt pond…we lost it. I have a few blurry pictures, unfortunately not great. BUT SO EXCITING!!! This is the first grasshopper sparrow we have had in the county. We weren’t even paying attention to birds in the field…just awesome luck to see an odd shaped sparrow dart under a bush.

While sorting through a flock in alders on the north side of the bridge, I noticed a large flycatcher pop up onto the wires that run just above the riparian on the south side of the bridge. I could see that it looked bright yellow below, but my momentary expectation that it would be a Tropical Kingbird was dispelled immediately as I got bins on it and saw a large Myiarchus with a bright yellow belly looking back at me. Instantly the hand-shaking adrenaline rush and the get-photos reflex were triggered, and after securing photos I ran to a better vantage with respect to lighting where I could also see the bird's back well enough to get an idea of the tertial pattern. A minute later the bird dropped down from the wire into the alders, and I made calls and so on to get the word out. I stayed until dusk with a large group of observers and, unfortunately, we were all unable to relocate the bird, although some thought they might have heard calls around sunset.

The bright and saturated rich lemon-yellow color of the belly was immediately obvious, so much so that (again) it was momentarily suggestive of Tropical Kingbird. Also immediately obvious were the very large size and, in particular, the rather large bill. Even in my first views, the large pale pinkish-yellowish zone at the base of the bill and the darkish gray upper chest and throat, contrasting sharply with the yellow lower chest and belly but not contrasting strongly with the remainder of the dark brownish head, were apparent too. In better lighting, these features were still apparent, in fact more obvious, and it was also possible to see crisp white lines at the top of the wing panel formed by white outer webs to the tertials. Although my views were not optimal for assessing the cleanness of these white markings, nor the exact extents of the white in each feather, I thought that the uppermost of these white lines appeared thicker and shorter than the lower 1–2. That is consistent with the tertial pattern expected in GCFL, with a nearly fully white outer web to the innermost (i.e., in the folded wing, uppermost) tertial. The wingbars were distinctly buff-tinged. The face, auriculars, crown, and remainder of the head were brownish and barely (if at all) darker than the throat, not contrastingly strongly with the throat. The tail was rather long, but so were the wings, making the tail not appear terribly long in proportion. I was unable to resolve details of rectrix pattern other than noting that the underside of the tail appeared uniformly rufous from a distance. 

The saturated yellow underparts, fairly sharp transition to the gray chest, dark tone of the gray chest and throat, minimal contrast between the color of the throat and that of the rest of the head, large bill with extensive pale zone at the base, and very bulky appearance are inconsistent with Ash-throated; while views of the tertials were not optimal, they still suggested the extensive white in the innermost tertial characteristic of GCFL and also inconsistent with Ash-throated. The saturation of the yellow below, the strong contrast with the fairly dark gray chest, the darkish throat, and the bill (being large but not massive and with an extensive pale base to the lower mandible) are suggestive of GCFL over Brown-crested. Photographs support all these features except for tertial pattern (tertials not visible in photos). It is worth noting that in the field this bird appeared still more richly colored below than the photos suggest.

After a few good years in the state (~4 each in 2020, 2021, 2023, ~8 in 2023), only one was recorded in 2025. This year there have been two so far, from Napa and Marin. This is an exceptionally late date; although several have stayed until the last day or two of October, there are no previous NorCal records in November and only a handful from the first week of November in SoCal.

A fairly cooperative bird working the willows south of the barn, first at (37.1315392, -122.3129582) and then later relocated with other observers at various spots in the willow patch. Initially detected by its scold, with short repeated nasal "rehr rehr rehr" calls each with a rising-then-falling cadence, unlike the scold of any common vireo. I am familiar with this scold and knew to look for a Philly Vireo immediately upon hearing it, but all I could see at first were two Hutton's, which was puzzling—the scold really sounded like a Philly and not like any Hutton's I have ever heard—and then the Philly popped out in front of me and provided good views as I followed it for the next fifteen minutes, and again when refound more than an hour later. It was rather slow-moving and sat still for periods, which explained why I struggled to see it at first; it was presumably sitting still somewhere obscured by vegetation. This was a moderately bright individual with a strong yellow wash to the underparts, clearly strongest on the throat and the upper part of the chest, becoming weaker toward the belly and flanks; a strongly patterned face with dark lores and a bold transocular, a rather short supercilium, a short and fairly stout bill, and a round head, all imparting a cute and somewhat feisty/spunky-looking facial expression, unlike the pale lores and blank face of WAVI; shorter tail and stockier build than WAVI; and distinctive scold, unlike the long slow dragged-out rasping scold calls of WAVI. This is a very late date, with only a handful (c. 3?) later records for NorCal. Within a mile of the Cascade Ck Bell's Vireo spot and within a quarter-mile of the Pie Ranch Blue-headed Vireo spot! First heard calling 30 feet north of the trail at: (37.8673771, -122.3102690), making squeaky Song Sparrow like bark calls, with single barks at first, followed by often double or triple barks. The bird later also gave the typical WIWR chatter call, similar to the recording in the Sibley app. The bird then came close, first giving good views in the willow clump on the north side of the trail at (37.8671807, -122.3103444), then crossing to the willow thicket at the southeast corner of the intersection of the main trail and the small spur trail (in the same spot where I found the first county record in 2024). Eventually moved south to (37.8664338, -122.3103592), before popping up again near the original location on the north side of the main trail. Last heard at 8:40am at about (37.8672398, -122.3105439). Pale overall, with a distinctly whitish throat and textured pale coloration extending across the entire side of the face, including the auriculars. The whitish pebbled/scaled texture extended downward from the throat, through the lower breast and upper flanks. The lower flanks were barred with dark blackish interspersed with thin white bands. Whitish supercilium, with a medium brown line extending rearward from the eye. The medium brown crown and nape merged with a brown to chestnut back and a short chestnut tail with dark barring. Tiny white spangles on the lesser and median wing coverts, brown and buff barring on the primaries. When brightly lit, the upper parts appeared almost rufous in color. This is purely speculative, but given that this bird was observed in the same location (sometimes perching in nearly identical spots in the same willows), this could be the same returning individual that I found in November, 2024 and which continued through March 2025. Interestingly, that bird had a distinctive depigmented (mostly white) left alula. Unfortunately, my photos didn't capture that feature well on the current bird. The 2024 bird was later accepted by CBRC ( a first record for the county), but was not detected in the winter of 2025/2026. See https://ebird.org/checklist/S203502632 for the 2024 observation. I got it in my bins for approximately 3 to 5 seconds at no more than 20 m distant.. flycatcher by shape and posture, sayornis by dipping tail. The underparts, which is what first grabbed my attention were very not whitish with a light yellow/cream wash, from the belly through breast to throat. Upper parts were a dark gray, paler than a black Phoebe. The bird never called and took off when a Cooper’s Hawk landed in the eucalyptus tree above the lawn. Spent the next hour and a half trying to relocate it,  doing laps from the Lawn to  the Museum garden. this is the first record of eastern Phoebe for Corona Hill. While rare,  sightings of the species are not unprecedented in late fall through early winter. One was  on Twin Peaks on 11/19-23/25. Perhaps a thorough search of the park later in the day will turn it up again.

Electric! A spectacular and ferocious-looking Mesoamerican megavireo initially at (37.7329629, -122.4987988), first in the madrone (?) outside the fence and then in the oak inside the Grizzle Bear enclosure. A short time later we had a Yellow-green Vireo 300 m away in shrubs around (37.7336260, -122.5014907), presumably the same individual; it was quite mobile and hard to stay on. A very large vireo, almost the size of a Hermit Thrush, with wings drooped and tail cocked, an immense bill and large head, bright greenish-yellow dorsum except for light blue-gray cap, highlighter yellow flanks and sides of chest, whitish strip including throat and extending down underparts, whitish supercilium, indistinct dark eyeline and lateral crown stripes. We missed photos the first time we saw this bird, despite decent looks for all three observers, but managed to photograph it the second time. Another rather strong year for this species in California; this is the ~8th in NorCal this year.

While listening to several longspurs rattling overhead, I heard another bird coming in from farther away giving distinct “keedle” calls, completely different from the Lapland rattle and tew calls. As it landed in front of me I noticed a big flash of white in its tail which was enough to convince me it was a Chestnut collar. Closer observation showed a longspur with a relatively drab appearance, lacking the dark auricular border of a Lapland but with a dark brown line behind the eye instead. This bird did not show any chestnut on its nape and was mostly a brown/buff color throughout with lots of streaking. Most of my observations occurred near  (37.6426606, -122.1499306). The bird flew south into the marsh and returned after a while, but then did so again and was not seen for the rest of the day. Photos and audio.

Fifth time was the charm for me for this continuing bird;  I think going out early helped.    Merlin picked up Brewer’s chips as I approached the first of the scrubby trees just after the first bench (7:10).   I froze and stood as I could see movement near the base of the tree, right on the trail’s edge.   At about 7:15 the Brewer’s Sparrow edged out onto the trail and I noticed a tiny pinkish bill, weak markings on face, streaks on top of the head, brownish-gray overall, with stripes on back and plain underside.  It looked like this bird had a suggestion of an eye-ring, but it didn’t stand out.   A minute later, a motorized bike screamed by, and the bird flew.
The bill tip and face tucked into reeds on back left part of the channel were the only visible parts of this continuing bird this morning at 8:05am.
